Money and Markets

Mispriced Countries

Eight economies on the verge. Index committees and IMF calendars are about to reprice whole markets on dates already printed. The question is which of the world's cheapest markets are cheap by mistake, and which are cheap because the risk is real.

By Josh Pilcher · Tuesday, November 10, 2026

The Bottom Line

Eight countries rank, and the ranking is not a list of the cheapest markets in the world. It is a list of markets whose price still belongs to an old label after the label has started to change. Vietnam ranks first and Nigeria second, because their catalysts are dated events on a calendar, an index upgrade phasing in on schedule and a frontier restoration already in effect, and because their multiples stay low even after you charge them honestly for their risk. Egypt is cheaper than both and ranks third, because cheapness alone is not the argument.

Argentina is the warning that runs under the whole report. A market that looked like the great mispricing of the decade reminded everyone in one week in November why it was cheap in the first place. The difference between a mispricing and a market correctly pricing risk is the only thing being judged here, country by country.

The Argument

A Country Gets Refiled Before It Gets Repriced

Index upgrades and IMF programme exits are dated, mechanical events. Money is required to move when they land. Prices, most of the time, move later.

There is a small committee you have probably never thought about that decides, in effect, what a country is. It works for an index provider, FTSE Russell or MSCI or S&P Dow Jones, and a few times a year it moves a name from one list to another. Frontier to emerging. Emerging to developed. Investable to unclassified.

The announcement reads like paperwork, which is exactly why it matters. Behind those lists sits the machinery of modern investing, trillions of dollars in funds that are required to own what the list contains and forbidden, by their own rules, from owning what it leaves out. When the committee moves a country, money does not get a vote. It gets an instruction, dated in advance, and it moves on schedule whether anyone believes in the country or not.

The IMF runs a slower version of the same machine. A programme starts, and a country borrows under supervision. A programme ends, and the supervision lifts on a printed date. Investors treat both moments as verdicts, and they price the country in front of them accordingly.

So a market price is rarely a price on a country. It is a price on the last category the country was filed under. Vietnam is still quoted as a frontier market even though FTSE began moving it into emerging markets in September. Greece is still quoted as a crisis story even though it is completing the first journey in MSCI history from developed to emerging and all the way back. Nigeria spent years quoted as uninvestable, a market the index had simply deleted, and it has now been written back in.

The underlying country changes slowly, the way countries do, through budgets and ports and power grids. The category changes on a single date. The price, caught between a slow reality and a sudden label, is where the opportunity lives.

It would be easy to stop there and buy whatever the committee is about to promote. That story, on its own, would be wrong. A promotion is not a verdict that a country is good. It is a verdict that a country is now legible to large pools of capital, that its settlement systems work and that foreigners can get in and, just as important, get out. The risk that kept a country in the lower category does not vanish on promotion day. It gets priced, in the return investors demand for holding the place at all.

That demand is measurable, and this report measures it before it ranks anything. For Poland the demand is about 10 percent a year in dollars. For Egypt and Pakistan it is close to 19 percent. A market trading at six times earnings sounds cheap until you understand that its buyers are, quite reasonably, demanding nearly a fifth of their money back every year for the risk. Then six times earnings stops sounding like a gift and starts sounding like a question. Can these earnings grow, in dollars, faster than that demand eats them? Every country below is that question, asked eight different ways.

The War That Moved Countries Backward

Every crossing in this report is happening against a war that is pushing other countries the other way. On 28 February 2026 the United States and Israel struck Iran. Iran retaliated by disrupting the Strait of Hormuz, and the IEA called it the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market.

Brent crude peaked near $126 a barrel. Saudi production fell about 30 percent in March 2026, to 7.25 million barrels a day, and crude exports fell by half that month. The IMF's October 2026 outlook works on the assumption that Hormuz shipping starts to resume in March 2027 and is broadly back to pre-war conditions by October 2027. On that assumption it still projects 2026 contractions of 16.7 percent for Kuwait, 16.0 percent for Iraq, 15.6 percent for Qatar and 3.3 percent for Saudi Arabia.

Keep that picture in mind. Saudi Arabia, which was building the region's great graduation story, falls off this list entirely. Egypt loses canal revenue at the exact moment it tries to stand without the IMF. And every oil importer below is being tested by an energy shock at the very moment it asks the market to believe it has changed. Graduation, in 2026, is not happening in calm weather. That is part of why the prices have not caught up, and part of why some of them should not.

The growth backdrop is strong enough to make the question worth asking. The IMF expects the world to grow 3.1 percent in 2026 and 3.4 percent in 2027. Against that, Vietnam grows at 8.4 percent, Uzbekistan at 7.8 percent, Egypt at 5.1 percent in the middle of an IMF programme. Growth alone settles nothing, and the proof sits just off the ranked list. India grows at 7.0 percent too, and its market trades at 22.8 times forward earnings, fully priced for the future it is having.

So read what follows as one argument in eight chapters. Something in each of these places has already changed. A date on a calendar will make that change official, and money will be required to act on it. The only question worth asking, country by country, is whether the price you can pay today already knows.

The Price of Risk

Cheap Is a Price. Mispriced Is a Price Measured Against Risk.

Before any country is praised for being cheap, it gets charged for its risk, in the open, from sourced parts.

The anchor is the United States 10 year Treasury, yielding 4.88 percent on 9 Nov 2026. On top of that sits the mature market equity risk premium of 4.23 percent, Aswath Damodaran's implied premium on the S&P 500 at 1 Jan 2026. On top of that sits each country's risk premium, from Damodaran's country default spreads table, last updated 5 Jan 2026.

Add the three together at a beta of 1.0 and you get an illustrative cost of equity in dollars. The word illustrative matters. These figures are derived from the sourced inputs above, not published anywhere as a set, and the beta of 1.0 is an assumption stated here, not an estimate found in a source. No size or illiquidity premium is added, which means the true bar for Nigeria, Uzbekistan and Pakistan is higher than the one printed.

Terminal growth is set at 3 percent in dollars for every country. That is an assumption, not a forecast. It is the same for all eight so that the comparison is honest: what separates these markets is the risk charge, not a growth story invented country by country.

Now read the result plainly. Nigeria, Egypt, Pakistan and Argentina need roughly 18 to 19 percent returns a year in dollars just to clear their cost of equity. A low multiple in any of them is only cheap if earnings grow fast enough, in dollar terms, to beat that number. Poland needs 10.21 percent. That is why Poland at 11.9 times earnings can be a better buy than Egypt at 5.74 times, and why the ranking in this report is not the ranking in the price chart above.

One more caution, and it is not small. The Damodaran figures are from January 2026, and spreads have moved since, Argentina's sharply. Treat every cost of equity below as a baseline, a floor under the true price of risk in November 2026, not as a live quote.

A warning about ETF target prices

The target prices quoted for country funds in this report need a warning label, because they are not what they look like. TipRanks, the ETF Research Center and MarketBeat do not publish a bank's opinion on a fund. They publish weighted averages of analyst targets on the stocks inside the fund. Those averages disagree with each other, sometimes wildly, and they can be stale. They are reported here as what they are, side by side, and never averaged into a single comforting number.

The disagreements are the finding. For the Argentina fund ARGT, TipRanks shows $114.76 and MarketBeat shows $73.67. For the Vietnam fund VNM, the ETF Research Center shows $23.96 and StockScan shows $16.86. Both pairs cannot be a consensus, so neither is treated as one.

For the Nigeria fund NGE, the Egypt fund EGPT, the Pakistan fund PAK and the Uzbekistan fund UzNIF, no consensus target was sourced at all. That is reported in their chapters as no coverage found. It is not a zero, and it is not filled in with an estimate.

Two famous targets are dead and are labelled dead wherever they appear. Goldman Sachs put a $47.80 to $52.20 range on the Brazil fund EWZ on 14 Oct 2026, conditional on a Bolsonaro win. Lula won, so the range is superseded. AKD's target of 263,800 for Pakistan's KSE-100 by December 2026 was overtaken by the correction of January to March 2026. It is superseded too.

No published JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley or Bank of America country index valuation model was found for Vietnam, Nigeria, Egypt, Poland, Greece or Uzbekistan in the searches behind this report. That is a not found result, not proof that none exists.

Rank 1 of Eight

Vietnam

The upgrade is done, the bigger one is next, and the price still belongs to the frontier market it left.

Access: VNM ETF (VanEck) · $17.12 on 9 Nov 2026

Vietnam is the clearest version of the story this report is telling, which is why it comes first. An economy that has spent a decade becoming the world's alternative factory floor has finally been recognised by the filing system. FTSE Russell began moving it from frontier to emerging in September 2026, in dated phases that complete in September 2027, and MSCI is the next and larger decision behind it.

Recognition, in this machinery, is a schedule of forced buying spread over a year, into a market foreigners own just 12.6 percent of and have been selling at a record pace. And the price still reads like the old country: about 11.7 times 2026 earnings for the index, and near 9 times once Vingroup, the conglomerate that makes up roughly a sixth of the index at more than 130 times earnings, is stripped out.

Old label, new country, a calendar of money that has to arrive. That is as close to a mechanical mispricing as equity markets offer. The distance between Vietnam and everything ranked below it is the distance between a schedule and a hope.

Catalyst and Timeline

  • 21 Sep 2026FTSE Russell: Frontier to Secondary Emerging, effective. Inclusion starts at 10%; 27 stocks entered the FTSE global index series, at about 0.49% weight in FTSE Emerging.
  • Mar 2027FTSE phase-in reaches 20%. The central counterparty framework is due by end 2026 and operational in the first quarter of 2027, the MSCI prerequisite.
  • Jun 2027FTSE reaches 35%. MSCI annual review: watch list entry expected in mid-2027 at the earliest. The government target is MSCI Emerging by 2030.
  • Sep 2027FTSE inclusion reaches 100%.

Inflow estimates vary so widely that the range is the finding: FTSE and HSBC models say $3.4bn to $6bn, the World Bank $3bn to $5bn, VinaCapital $5bn to $6bn, CICC $19bn to $20bn. The World Bank estimates MSCI inflows could be three to four times the FTSE figure.

Economic Stakes

The IMF expects growth of 8.4 percent in 2026 and 7.5 percent in 2027, on GDP of $542.1bn, making Vietnam the fastest growing large emerging economy in this report. The domestic print is running hotter: output grew 9.95 percent year on year in the third quarter of 2026 and 9.01 percent over the first nine months.

About VND350trn of public investment was still to be disbursed against a deadline of end January 2027, a fiscal tailwind that lands in the same window as the index phase-in.

Valuation and Mispricing

The VN-Index trades at about 11.7 times 2026 earnings and 10.7 times 2027 earnings. Excluding Vingroup, those fall to about 9.0 times and 8.1 times. Trailing price to earnings is 13.5 times, price to book excluding Vingroup is 1.57 times, the lowest valuation zone in five years.

The distortion matters. Vingroup is about 16 percent of index weight at over 130 times earnings. The headline multiple overstates what the rest of the market costs, and anyone buying the index is materially long one conglomerate.

Currency

The dong is managed. No large currency mispricing is claimed for Vietnam, because no fair value gap against history was sourced. Any argument that the dong is cheap is, on the record behind this report, unsourced. The thesis is an equity and index thesis, not a currency one.

Analyst View

For the VNM fund, the ETF Research Center, on closes of 9 Nov 2026, shows a holdings-derived target of $23.96, about 40 percent above the price, rated Overweight. StockScan's average target is $16.86, slightly below the price. Both are weighted averages of targets on the fund's holdings from different methods. They are shown side by side and not averaged.

On the flagship stock Vinamilk, the two local brokers disagree by 22 percent: ACBS said Buy with a target of VND72,000 by end 2026 on 11 May 2026, using a blend of discounted cash flow and multiples, with no discount rate disclosed in the summary retrieved. Guotai Haitong said Accumulate at VND59,000 on 13 Oct 2026.

DCF Inputs

Risk free 4.88% · Mature ERP 4.23% · Country risk premium 3.90% · Total ERP 8.13%
Cost of equity (beta 1.0) = 13.01% · Terminal growth 3%, an assumption

Market net profit growth is forecast at 37.8 percent for 2026. At a 13.01 percent cost of equity, the market needs sustained double digit earnings growth in dollars to justify even a mid-teens multiple. The 2026 forecast clears that bar. A 37.8 percent growth rate is not sustainable and must not be extrapolated. The index dividend yield was not sourced and is not estimated here.

Risks

  • Vingroup concentration: one group, about a sixth of the index, at over 130 times earnings.
  • United States tariffs and trade exposure. The manufacturing shift is the thesis and the vulnerability at once.
  • Dong depreciation if the Federal Reserve stays tight.
  • An MSCI watch list delay if the central counterparty slips past the first quarter of 2027.
  • A property sector overhang that has not fully cleared.

Strongest Bear Case

Foreign investors have sold a record $4.5bn in 2026. The market is not overlooked, it is being actively exited, and the FTSE inflow estimates are so wide they are not a forecast. The ex-Vingroup multiple is flattered by banks and industrials whose earnings are cyclically high.

What would falsify the thesis: MSCI watch list entry delayed beyond June 2027; foreign net selling continuing through the March 2027 FTSE phase-in; index earnings growth printing below 10 percent in 2027 while the multiple compresses further.

Rank 2 of Eight

Nigeria

Written back into the index, with a currency that held its float and banks at half of book value.

Access: NGE ETF (Global X) · $3.74 on 6 Nov 2026 · Assets of just $11.07m

Nigeria's crossing started from further back than anyone else's on this list, which is what makes it so instructive. This was not a market priced cheaply. It was a market the index had deleted, filed as unclassified after years of currency controls that made it impossible to take money out, the one sin the filing system does not forgive.

Then, beginning in 2023, Nigeria did the hard things in the right order. It abolished the fuel subsidy, abandoned its thicket of exchange rates, floated the naira and let it fall, and tightened policy until inflation, which peaked near 35 percent, came down to about 15 percent. The float held. Reserves climbed to $55bn, an eighteen year high. In September, FTSE wrote Nigeria back into the frontier index.

What holds Nigeria at second place, and what any honest telling has to sit with, is that the market has already risen about 75 percent in dollar terms this year. The first and easiest part of being refiled has already been paid for. What remains is the harder claim, that Nigerian earnings are real earnings and not the one-time windfall of a devaluation. That claim now has to be proved in results rather than in reform announcements.

Catalyst and Timeline

  • 2023Fuel subsidy abolished, the multi-tier exchange rate system abandoned, the naira floated. The central bank tightened aggressively.
  • 1 Jun 2026Settlement moves to T+1, a technical prerequisite for the index return.
  • 21 Sep 2026FTSE Russell restores Nigeria from Unclassified to Frontier Market. Thirty-one stocks enter the frontier series, six of them the Frontier 50: Aradel, Dangote Cement, FirstHoldCo, GTCO, MTN Nigeria and Zenith Bank.
  • 2026 to 2027Cordros Securities projects $840m to $1.04bn of passive inflows from the reclassification.

Economic Stakes

Inflation fell from 34.8 percent in December 2024 to 15.2 percent in December 2025. Real GDP grew 4.43 percent year on year in the second quarter of 2026, and the IMF expects 4.2 percent in 2026 and 4.3 percent in 2027, on GDP of $386.7bn.

Measured in dollars, GDP rose from $290.5bn to $386.7bn in a year, a gain of 33.1 percent and the largest in Africa. Say it plainly: that jump is mostly a currency effect, the result of the naira stabilising, not real growth alone.

Valuation and Mispricing

The NGX trades at 6.92 times earnings against a ten year average of 11.3 times. The banks average 0.49 times book value despite profit growth of 30 to 50 percent and returns on equity of 20 to 30 percent: UBA at 2.4 times earnings, GTCO at 6.2 times, Stanbic IBTC at 5.7 times.

The offset is real. The market is up 74.7 percent in dollar terms this year to 6 Oct 2026. Foreigners were only about 11 to 12 percent of NGX transactions in the first half of 2026, down from 27 percent a year earlier, and of $10.4bn of capital inflows in the first quarter only about 1 percent went into equities. The market is cheap and still largely unowned, but the entry point is worse than it was in January.

Currency

The naira traded at about N1,349 per dollar on 5 Nov 2026, against about N1,391 at the end of January. The float has held for three years, and reserves at an eighteen year high support it. A claim that the naira is undervalued on a purchasing power basis was not sourced, so no fair value number is asserted.

Analyst View

There is no analyst consensus and no price target for the NGE fund. Its stated distribution yield of 16.04 percent is a distribution figure on an $11m fund, not a forecast, and should be treated with caution. Targets from local brokers for the flagship Nigerian banks were not sourced either. Both gaps are reported as No coverage found, and nothing is filled in.

DCF Inputs

Risk free 4.88% · Mature ERP 4.23% · Country risk premium 8.41% · Total ERP 12.64%
Cost of equity (beta 1.0) = 17.52% · Terminal growth 3%, an assumption

At a 17.52 percent cost of equity and 3 percent terminal growth, a 6.92 times multiple prices in roughly flat to negative earnings growth in dollars, forever. The thesis is that bank profit growth of 30 to 50 percent, even if it halves, clears that bar. The index dividend yield was not sourced. If oil falls below the fiscal breakeven, the growth and the naira go with it.

Risks

  • The oil price, which the IMF flags as the key determinant for Nigeria.
  • Security in the north.
  • Reform reversal risk around the 2027 election cycle.
  • The naira weakening again if reserves are drawn down to defend it.
  • The war's effect on oil cuts both ways for an exporter.

Strongest Bear Case

A 6.92 times multiple after a 75 percent dollar rally is not a mispricing. It is a market pricing in that bank earnings are a one-off devaluation windfall, foreign exchange revaluation gains that will not repeat, and that the FTSE inflow of $840m to $1.04bn is trivial against a market capitalisation of N158.81trn.

What would falsify the thesis: foreign participation in NGX transactions staying below about 12 percent through 2027 despite FTSE inclusion; the naira weakening back above N1,600 per dollar; bank returns on equity falling below 15 percent in 2027 results.

Rank 3 of Eight

Egypt

The cheapest market in the set, at the end of an IMF programme, with the hardest risk charge on the page.

Access: EGPT ETF (VanEck) · Assets of about $37m · No consensus coverage found

Egypt is the test of whether you actually believe this report's argument, or only believe it when it is comfortable. By the simple arithmetic of cheapness it should rank first, and it is not close: 5.74 times forward earnings and a dividend yield of 8.59 percent, the cheapest MSCI country index in the set.

And the crossing is real. The pound was floated in March 2024 and stayed floated. Inflation has fallen from around 40 percent to 13.9 percent. Remittances hit a record. The government ran a primary surplus of 4.9 percent of GDP, ahead of the target the IMF set. On 15 December the $8bn IMF programme ends, and the prime minister has said there will not be another one, which is either the declaration of a country graduating from supervision or the removal of the supervisor at the worst possible moment.

That ambiguity is the thesis. Egypt refinances more than 30 percent of GDP every year and spends roughly 60 percent of its revenue on interest. Third place is not a hedge. It is the argument, applied honestly to its hardest case.

Catalyst and Timeline

  • Mar 2024The pound is floated and the IMF programme is expanded to $8bn. The Ras El Hekma deal brings $35bn from the UAE's ADQ (Feb 2024).
  • 4 Oct 2026Prime Minister Madbouly says there will be no new IMF programme, and promises an independent economic plan to 2045.
  • 15 Dec 2026The IMF programme ends. The final reviews unlock about $2.3bn. The IMF's seventh review put growth at 5.0 percent in the third quarter of fiscal 2025/26.

The one counter-catalyst: FTSE placed Egypt on its watch list in September 2025 for a possible downgrade from Secondary Emerging to Frontier, because the market fails the minimum securities count. A downgrade would trigger outflows, the exact opposite of the Vietnam and Nigeria dynamic.

Economic Stakes

The IMF expects growth of 5.1 percent in 2026 and 4.7 percent in 2027, on GDP of $442.9bn. Remittances reached a record $33.9bn in the first eight months of 2026, up 27 percent year on year. Reserves stood at about $55bn at the end of June 2026.

Suez Canal revenue was $567.1m in August 2026, with the fiscal year running at $4.67bn against the $10.25bn record of 2023. The war halved the canal, and the recovery so far is partial.

Valuation and Mispricing

The MSCI Egypt Index, on its factsheet of 30 Oct 2026, trades at a price to earnings of 5.60 times, a forward multiple of 5.74 times, price to book of 1.93 times and a dividend yield of 8.59 percent. One month earlier the trailing multiple was 4.62 times. This is the cheapest MSCI country index in the set.

Two warnings belong inside the valuation, not under it. The index has only three constituents, so concentration and currency history explain part of the discount; it is not a diversified market. And its one year return in dollars was 3.65 percent, with the year to date slightly negative, so the cheapness has not yet started to close.

Currency

The pound was floated in March 2024. It still depreciated 15 percent earlier in 2026, during $9.5bn of foreign portfolio outflows. A claim that the pound is now undervalued on a fair value basis was not sourced, and none is made.

Analyst View

No consensus target was sourced for the EGPT fund, and no flagship Egyptian equity target was sourced either. Both are reported as No coverage found. The sovereign view that matters here belongs to a rating agency: S&P affirmed Egypt at B/B with a stable outlook on 13 Oct 2026.

DCF Inputs

Risk free 4.88% · Mature ERP 4.23% · Country risk premium 9.71% · Total ERP 13.94%
Cost of equity (beta 1.0) = 18.82% · Terminal growth 3%, an assumption

The dividend yield of 8.59 percent, the highest sourced in the ranked set, covers just under half of the 18.82 percent required return on its own. The thesis therefore needs real earnings growth in dollars of roughly 10 percent or more on top, sustained. Index earnings growth was not sourced. That high bar, and nothing else, is why the cheapest market in the set ranks third.

Risks

  • Gross financing needs above 30 percent of GDP, every year.
  • Interest at about 60 percent of revenue in 2026/27 and 53 percent in 2027/28.
  • A possible FTSE downgrade to Frontier.
  • Suez revenues still less than half their 2023 record.
  • The programme exit removes the IMF anchor itself.

Strongest Bear Case

A 5.74 times multiple against an 18.82 percent cost of equity is not cheap. It is the market correctly pricing a sovereign that spends 60 percent of its revenue on interest and must refinance more than 30 percent of GDP every year, with no IMF programme after 15 December 2026. The 8.59 percent yield is a trap if the pound depreciates again.

What would falsify the thesis: a FTSE downgrade to Frontier; a failed post-programme debt auction or a return to double digit monthly currency depreciation; interest rising above 65 percent of revenue in fiscal 2026/27.

Rank 4 of Eight

Poland

The same story with the risk mostly gone: a dated developed market upgrade at half the world's multiple.

Access: EPOL ETF (iShares) · About $43 on 9 Nov 2026

Poland shows what the same story looks like when the risk is mostly gone, and the comparison is clarifying. Here is an economy that has crossed the trillion dollar line, the fastest growing large economy in the European Union, already treated as developed by FTSE Russell and Stoxx since 2018, now formally upgraded by S&P Dow Jones with effect from September 2027, and still waiting on MSCI, the last and largest prize.

It trades at 11.9 times forward earnings against 22 times for the world. The return investors demand for holding it is just 10.21 percent, the lowest on this list, because Poland's dangers are the ordinary dangers of a rich country: debt drifting toward 68 percent of GDP and defence spending at 4.8 percent of GDP, rather than the existential ones further up the page.

That safety cuts both ways. Foreigners already account for nearly three quarters of trading in Warsaw, so nobody is discovering Poland, and earnings are expected to grow only about 5 percent. Poland is on this list not as a speculation but as a control group. It proves the ranking is not in love with danger.

Economic Stakes

GDP grew 3.6 percent in 2025 and 3.9 percent year on year in the second quarter of 2026. Inflation is expected near 2.9 percent in 2027, and the central bank rate of about 4.25 percent is expected to be cut toward 3.5 to 4.0 percent.

Defence spending is 4.8 percent of GDP, $55bn in 2026 against $15bn in 2022, the highest share in NATO. It is a growth driver and a fiscal strain at the same time, and it is the main reason public debt, near 60 percent of GDP now, is heading toward 68 percent by 2027.

Valuation and Mispricing

MSCI Poland trades at about 11.9 times forward earnings, against 22.0 times for the MSCI All World and 17.7 times for emerging markets. The local WIG30 total return index is at about 10.5 times, a 28 percent discount to broader Europe, yielding about 4.2 percent.

Frame it honestly: foreigners were a record 73 percent of Warsaw main market trading in the first half of 2026. This is not an underweight story like Vietnam or Nigeria. It is a rerating story, a weaker form of mispricing, and the momentum check agrees: the WIG rose 47 percent in local terms in 2025 and crossed 100,000 for the first time.

Currency

The zloty carries no thesis here. No fair value gap was sourced for it, and none is claimed. Poland's case is multiple expansion plus domestic flows, with no currency leg.

Analyst View

For the EPOL fund, the ETF Research Center, on closes of 8 Nov 2026, shows a holdings-derived target of $44.59, about 4 percent above the price. Modest, and honestly so. A single contributor's $60 target, about 35 percent higher, is one bull's view and is not cited as consensus anywhere in this report.

The lowest cost of equity in the set is why an 11.9 times multiple here is less demanding than 5.74 times in Egypt. The constraint is growth: WIG net profit growth of only about 5 percent is expected. At a 10.21 percent bar, 5 percent growth plus a 4.2 percent yield roughly clears it, with little margin for error. Poland is the quality leg of the list: lower upside, far lower probability of a zero.

Risks

  • Debt heading to about 68 percent of GDP by 2027.
  • Defence spending as a permanent fiscal strain.
  • The 2025 rally means the easy rerating is done.
  • The MSCI upgrade is three to five years away, not dated.

Strongest Bear Case

Poland is not mispriced. It is fairly priced for 5 percent earnings growth. The S&P upgrade was announced in August 2026, so the market has had months to price it, and a 73 percent foreign share of trading shows the trade is crowded, not overlooked.

What would falsify the thesis: MSCI explicitly declining to put Poland on its watch list; WIG earnings growth printing below 3 percent in 2027; the deficit pushing debt above 70 percent of GDP.

Rank 5 of Eight

Greece

The first developed to emerging to developed journey in MSCI history, and mostly already paid for.

Access: GREK ETF (Global X) · About $79 to $82 in early Nov 2026

No country on earth carries this report's argument in its own biography the way Greece does. Within living memory it was a developed market. Then the euro crisis tore it out of that category and MSCI demoted it to emerging in 2013, a rich country formally refiled as a poor one. Now it is travelling back.

FTSE and STOXX restored it to developed status in September 2026. In May 2027 MSCI completes the journey. The substance behind the symbolism is genuinely impressive: a primary surplus of 4.9 percent of GDP from a state that once could not count its own deficit, investment grade ratings from every agency, a market at 9.4 times earnings yielding 5.6 percent.

And yet Greece ranks only fifth, for a reason that goes to the heart of the whole exercise. A crossing only pays if you arrive before the price learns the new label, and Athens has risen 162 percent since 2021. The market has learned. What is left is a slow economy growing at about 2 percent, carrying debt of 136 percent of GDP, waiting for a promotion that was announced in March and surprises nobody. Greece is proof that the story works. It is also proof that a true story, bought late, is just a story.

The IMF expects growth of about 2.0 percent in 2026, the lowest in the ranked set. The Bank of Greece put first quarter growth at 2.0 percent year on year, against 0.5 percent for the euro area. Inflation averaged 3.6 percent over January to August 2026, and unemployment sits between 7.7 and 8.9 percent.

S&P, Fitch and DBRS rate Greece BBB with a stable outlook and Moody's rates it Baa3: investment grade everywhere, a sentence that was unthinkable a decade ago. Market capitalisation is about 140 to 150 billion euros, roughly half of GDP.

The FTSE ASE index is forecast at 9.4 times FY2026 earnings and 8.4 times FY2027, at 1.2 times book, with dividend yields of 5.6 percent rising to 6.1 percent Dated. Those forecasts are thirteen months old, no newer equivalent was found, and they are flagged at every appearance for that reason. The Athens market trades at a discount of more than 30 percent to its pre-crisis history and to European benchmarks on earnings and cash flow multiples.

The offset caps the rank: the ASE is up 162 percent cumulatively since 2021 and 44.19 percent in 2025 alone, a five year compound rate of 21.3 percent. Anyone buying the MSCI upgrade in November 2026 is buying it after a tripling.

Currency

The euro. There is no currency thesis, by construction. Greece's case stands or falls on the rerating and the fiscal record alone.

Rank 6 of Eight

Brazil

A fifth of the market's value gone in a day, on an election result it had priced at one chance in five.

Access: EWZ ETF (iShares) · $32.61 on 9 Nov 2026 · Down 25.1% in one month

Brazil is the one name here whose crossing ran in reverse, overnight. Going into the runoff on 25 October, prediction markets gave Flávio Bolsonaro roughly a 78 percent chance of winning, investors had positioned for fiscal consolidation, and the market had quietly filed Brazil under a future that did not happen. Lula won.

The next day the main Brazil fund fell about 20 percent, because a price built for one country has to be rebuilt, in a hurry and without much information, for another. What the rebuilding produced is worth pausing on: 9.5 times forward earnings, a 5.3 percent dividend yield, and a real policy rate near 8.8 percent, numbers that would look like value in any screen.

But Brazil teaches the report's hardest lesson in its purest form, because Brazil has looked like value for most of a decade and has stayed that way for a reason anyone can read. Gross debt is about 83 percent of GDP and has risen eleven points in under four years. Interest alone consumes 8.9 percent of GDP. The selloff was not the market misunderstanding Brazil. It was the market repricing, correctly, the probability that Brazil ever escapes that arithmetic. The case for owning it now is narrow: that a fall of a fifth in a day overcorrects even bad news. It is a trade on the size of a reaction, not a belief in a crossing, and it is ranked accordingly.

Catalyst and Timeline

  • 4 Oct 2026First round: Flávio Bolsonaro 47.03 percent, Lula 45.16 percent. Prediction markets gave Bolsonaro 77 to 78 percent for the runoff, and a Citi survey found 80 percent of investors expected a fall of 5 percent or more on a Lula win.

Economic Stakes

The IMF expects growth of 1.9 percent in 2026; Lombard Odier expects 1.8 percent in 2026 and 1.6 percent in 2027, the slowest in the ranked set after Greece. The stakes here are not growth. They are the debt path: 83 percent of GDP and rising, with 8.9 percent of GDP spent on interest, crowding out nearly everything else a state does.

Valuation and Mispricing

The Ibovespa trades at 9.5 times twelve month forward earnings with a forecast 2026 dividend yield of 5.3 percent. Bank of America in July 2026 had Brazil at 8.5 times against a historical average of 10.6 times, a discount of 20 percent to its own history and 18 percent to emerging markets, the widest in Latin America. Yardeni put the MSCI Brazil forward multiple at 8.6 times on 18 Sep 2026.

Two rival reads present themselves, and they can be separated by evidence. Read one: the selloff overcorrected, and commodity earnings plus a very high real rate carry the position while the fiscal question stays open. Read two: the market is pricing the debt correctly, as it has for a decade. The deciding condition is the 2027 budget. A primary balance path that stabilises debt below 85 percent of GDP settles it for read one. Another year of drift settles it for read two.

Currency

The real stood at 5.04 per dollar on 23 Oct 2026. No fair value claim for it was sourced. The Selic rate of 13.75 percent is a carry argument, payment for holding the currency, not evidence that the currency or the market is mispriced. The two should not be conflated.

Analyst View

Goldman Sachs, on 14 Oct 2026, put a theoretical EWZ range of $47.80 to $52.20 on the fund if rate spreads returned to recent lows, with earnings per share of about $4.40. Superseded That range was conditional on a Bolsonaro win. Citing it after 25 October would be misleading; it is shown only so that nobody cites it at you. Lombard Odier, after the result, called the selloff excessive and kept its preference for Brazilian equities, with no price target.

On Petrobras, where real coverage exists, fourteen analysts average a Buy with a target of $23.89, about 29 percent above the close of 6 Nov 2026. Goldman Sachs rates it Buy at $24 and Citi Hold at $22.

Brazil is the one ranked thesis where the valuation arithmetic and the politics are the same sentence.

Risks

  • Political: a Lula government facing a hostile Congress.

Brazil has been cheap at eight to nine times earnings for most of the last decade, and it stayed cheap because the fiscal trajectory is unsustainable. The market is not mispricing Lula. It is pricing the debt.

Rank 7 of Eight

Uzbekistan

The fastest reform story in the set, with no index, no fund on a US exchange, and access itself as the opportunity.

Access: UzNIF, listed in London and Tashkent · No country ETF exists

Uzbekistan has not been refiled yet, because for practical purposes it was never filed at all, and that absence is the opportunity in its rawest form. There is no MSCI index for it and no country fund on a United States exchange, because until very recently there was barely a market to measure: a stock exchange worth about $20bn inside a $178bn economy growing at 7.8 percent.

What changed is that the state decided to sell itself, carefully and in public. In May 2026 the Uzbekistan National Investment Fund, holding minority stakes in thirteen to eighteen state enterprises and managed by Franklin Templeton, listed in Tashkent and London. It raised $604m, was four times oversubscribed, drew $300m of cornerstone money from BlackRock and Franklin Templeton, and rose 26 percent in its first six weeks, while still trading about 10 percent below the value of what it owns at the end of June.

Around that single event an architecture is being built at speed: a capital markets law, a Nasdaq partnership to modernise the exchange, six more portfolio listings planned by the end of 2028, and an application to join the World Trade Organization that has cleared bilateral talks with thirty-three of thirty-four members. None of that makes Uzbekistan safe. The state is still both the seller of the assets and the referee of the market. But of every name in this report, Uzbekistan is where the distance between the economy that exists and the market that represents it is widest.

Rank 8 of Eight

Pakistan

Stabilisation at eight times earnings, after a correction that showed how quickly the story can finish.

Access: PAK ETF (Global X) · Assets of about $11m · No consensus coverage found

Pakistan closes the list because it is where the argument runs out of road, and a ranking that cannot show you its own edge is not worth trusting. The surface case is familiar by now and genuinely attractive: an IMF programme holding, a staff level agreement reached on 7 October, reserves rebuilding, and a market at about 8.4 times forward earnings yielding more than 6 percent.

But stand back and look at the shape of it. This market roughly quadrupled in three years on stabilisation alone, peaked in January, and then fell about 23 percent in six weeks: the behaviour of a momentum trade discovering it had finished its story, rather than a mispricing waiting to be found. Growth is 3.6 percent, the second slowest in the set. The return demanded for the risk is 18.82 percent, the joint highest. And the target that anchored the optimistic case now sits nearly 60 percent above where the market actually closed in October.

Pakistan may stabilise its way to something better, and the October agreement is a real step. But stabilisation is a country stopping getting worse. It is not yet a country becoming something else, and this report's whole claim is that only the second of those deserves to be called a mispricing.

That is a momentum market, not a mispriced one, and the 8.4 times multiple is struck against earnings that include a post-stabilisation sugar high. The bull case's anchor target is already 58 percent above the market.

What would falsify the bear case: Board approval of the October agreement followed by a sustained recovery above the January 2026 peak of 189,166 on rising volumes; reserves above $25bn; inflation below 8 percent in 2027.

Not Ranked

The Other Side of the Same Argument

A crossing can reverse. A label can be withdrawn. These six were considered, and each one failed for a reason that teaches you what the eight survivors still have to do.

Dropped, November 2026

Argentina

The fundamentals that made the bull case are real: monthly inflation down from 25.5 percent in December 2023 to 1.9 percent in September 2026, back to back primary surpluses for the first time in decades, growth of 4.4 percent in 2025, a $20bn IMF programme, and a market at 9.2 times forward earnings against a 10.4 times historical average.

Then, in the week of 5 to 7 Nov 2026, JP Morgan's country risk measure spiked to 925 to 939 basis points, the highest since October 2025, and the market-implied probability of President Milei's re-election collapsed from about 90 percent in July 2026 to about 45 percent in early November. Argentina carries about $25bn of hard currency obligations due in 2027, the IMF's third review produced no staff level agreement, and the US Treasury's $20bn support package was perceived to be at risk after the US midterm elections Election outcome not independently verified.

Verdict: a binary bet on the 2027 election with $25bn of 2027 maturities is not a mispricing. The analyst record shows the staleness plainly: TipRanks' holdings-derived target for the ARGT fund is $114.76 and MarketBeat's is $73.67, a disagreement of about 55 points, and both predate the risk spike. What would change the verdict: country risk back below about 600 basis points and holding for a quarter, an IMF staff level agreement on the third review, and the YPF, Eni and XRG liquefied natural gas investment decision signing on 26 to 30 Nov 2026 as scheduled.

Value Trap Candidate

Turkey

The cheapness is genuine. Turkish equities sit at a discount of about 57 percent to peers on 2027 earnings, and Gedik Investment's strategy report of 13 Oct 2026 sets a BIST-100 target of 19,380, about 58 percent above the market, with inflation of 29.7 percent in October 2026 and a policy rate cut to 36 percent on 22 Oct.

It fails anyway. On 17 Sep 2026 the capital markets board halted or liquidated 131 funds covering about 456,000 investors, and the index fell 14.87 percent in a month. S&P Dow Jones has frozen index changes on Turkish stocks and placed the country on its classification watch list. Disinflation is stalling, with monthly inflation of 2.58 percent in October, above expectations. The illustrative cost of equity is 13.77 percent.

Verdict: a 57 percent discount is the market pricing the possibility that the index itself stays frozen. What would change it: removal from the S&P Dow Jones watch list, a clean and uncontested fund sector, and inflation below 25 percent by mid-2027.

Thesis Suspended by the War

Saudi Arabia

Before the war, Vision 2030 was delivering: non-oil activity at 55 percent of GDP in 2025, foreign direct investment of $35.5bn against $7.5bn in 2017, and 93 percent of 2025 targets met or exceeded. Then March 2026 cut production by about 30 percent and halved crude exports in a single month.

The IMF's October 2026 outlook projects GDP down 3.3 percent in 2026, and the Finance Ministry's preliminary figures are worse, a contraction of 3.6 percent with a deficit of SAR245bn. The TASI index, near 10,590 on 6 Oct 2026, trades at 15.4 times earnings: not cheap even before the war discount is debated. Aramco keeps a Buy consensus, an average target of SAR30.20 from eighteen analysts, with Goldman Sachs at SAR34, but one stock's rating does not rescue a suspended country thesis. The cost of equity, 9.89 percent, is the lowest in this report, and it does not matter while the thesis depends on a strait.

Verdict: a recovery story for 2027 and 2028, contingent on Hormuz shipping resuming from March 2027, which is an IMF assumption and not a fact. Not a current mispricing.

Growth, Not Mispricing

India

The growth is the best in the large economy world, 7.0 percent in both 2026 and 2027 on the IMF's numbers, on GDP of about $4.15trn. The price is the problem. The Nifty trades at 22.8 times forward earnings, priced for earnings growth above 18 percent against delivery of 8 to 11 percent, and MSCI India at 18.4 times forward against 8.7 times for emerging markets as a whole. Foreign portfolio investors have been net sellers in 2026.

Verdict: at 22.8 times, the mispricing, if there is one, is on the downside. India is the control case for the whole report: growth at a full price is not an opportunity, however good the growth is.

Dropped, Negative Catalyst

Indonesia

On 15 Oct 2026 MSCI proposed reclassifying Indonesia from Emerging to Standalone, bypassing Frontier entirely, citing opacity, concentrated ownership, suspected coordinated trading and weak enforcement. The consultation runs to 30 Apr 2027, with a decision by 30 Jun 2027. The Jakarta index fell 8 to 11.6 percent on 16 Oct 2026, its worst day since January 1998, trading was halted, and the rupiah hit a record low near 18,000 per dollar.

MSCI Indonesia's index weight has collapsed from 1.16 percent in December 2025 to 0.43 percent in September 2026, and UBS estimates about $4bn of passive and up to $15bn of active outflows if the downgrade lands. Jakarta's response, disclosing holders of 1 percent or more, a 15 percent minimum free float and the exclusion of about eighty concentrated stocks, is real reform under duress. At 8.1 times forward earnings the market is cheap, and classification risk still dominates. The cost of equity is 11.57 percent.

Verdict: the mirror image of Vietnam, same region and opposite index direction. Avoid unless MSCI itself verifies the reforms.

Honourable Mention

Kenya

Kenya holds the cheapest stock level numbers in the whole report: Equity Group at about four times expected 2027 earnings, KCB at about three and a half times, dividend yields near 7 to 8 percent, and Safaricom at about 10.5 times with an earnings margin near 57 percent. Growth runs near 5 percent, reserves cover six to seven months of imports, and the central bank has cut its policy rate ten times since mid-2024, from 13.00 to 8.75 percent. Kingdom Securities rates Safaricom a long term Buy with a fair value of KES38.50 and KCB a Buy with a target of KES119.15.

It is held back by three facts: the cheapness is stock specific rather than index wide, inflation is re-accelerating, from 4.4 percent in March 2026 to 7.3 percent in October, and there is no IMF programme, with a general election due in August 2027. The cost of equity is 18.82 percent.

Verdict: a 2027 story, not a 2026 one. It leads the watchlist below.

Two more names were surfaced and set aside as mentions only. Ethiopia, growing at 9.2 to 10.2 percent with a stock exchange launched in January 2025, carries the highest cost of equity in the research at 20.77 percent and remains very early and illiquid. Sri Lanka, in a post-default recovery under a $3bn IMF programme ending in early 2027, trades near 11.5 times earnings while inflation re-accelerates. Neither is ranked and neither is priced here.

Watchlist

The Dates That Decide

Every thesis in this report was bought with a calendar attached. These are the dated tests, in order, that confirm the rankings or kill them.

Stand far enough back and the eight chapters above stop looking like eight separate trades and start looking like one event photographed from eight angles: the world is resorting its countries. Vietnam and Indonesia sit in the same region and the same asset class, and one is being promoted into emerging markets while the other is threatened with expulsion from them. Greece and Turkey share a sea, and one is rejoining the developed world while the other's index is frozen by its own regulators. The unit of analysis is no longer the asset class. It is the individual country's direction of travel, and direction of travel is something a careful reader can actually judge, date by date.

  • 126 to 30 November 2026: Argentina's gas decision. The YPF, Eni and XRG liquefied natural gas final investment decision is targeted for this window, followed by the second RIGI investment round on 2 December. A signature on schedule is the first evidence that the November risk spike was a scare rather than a verdict.
  • 215 December 2026: Egypt stands alone. The $8bn IMF programme ends and the final reviews unlock about $2.3bn. The first debt auctions and the first month of currency trading after that date are the real review. Watch also for any FTSE decision on the Frontier downgrade watch.
  • 3End of January 2027: Vietnam's spending deadline. About VND350trn of public investment is due to be disbursed by now. Delivery confirms the growth print behind the upgrade; a slip says the 9 percent quarters were the peak.
  • 4First quarter of 2027: Vietnam's counterparty test. The central counterparty must be operational for MSCI to move. In March the FTSE phase-in reaches 20 percent, the first dated check on whether foreign selling finally turns, and the IMF's assumption has Hormuz shipping starting to resume.
  • 530 April and 30 June 2027: Indonesia's verdict. MSCI's consultation closes in April and its reclassification decision lands by the end of June. A reprieve reopens a market down by a third; a Standalone ruling confirms the drop.
  • 6May 2027: Greece completes the journey. MSCI reclassifies Greece to Developed at the May Index Review. The test is not the promotion, it is whether the Athens market, up 162 percent since 2021, holds its multiple once the last mechanical buyer has bought.
  • 7June 2027: MSCI's annual review. The earliest window for Vietnam's watch list entry, and the FTSE phase-in reaches 35 percent the same month. A Vietnam omission here delays the second leg of the first ranked thesis by a full year.
  • 8August 2027: Kenya votes. The general election decides whether the cheapest banks in this research get their rerating or their risk premium. Watch for an IMF programme agreement before the vote; without one, Kenya stays an honourable mention.
  • 9September 2027: two completions. Vietnam's FTSE inclusion reaches 100 percent and Poland's S&P Dow Jones developed market upgrade takes effect. By this date the two most mechanical theses in the report will have been fully tested by the flows they promised.
  • 10Through 2027 and 2028: the slow proofs. Pakistan must win IMF Board approval for the October agreement and rebuild reserves toward $25bn. Brazil's 2027 budget must show debt stabilising below 85 percent of GDP. Uzbekistan owes six portfolio IPOs by the end of 2028 and a WTO answer from the Cameroon ministerial. None of these is a single date, which is exactly why those countries rank where they rank.
